archetype.name: Lost Season (shooting without the rest)
archetype.definition: A team coming off five straight winning seasons fell to 32-50 and 23rd on the site, and even that record overstated how good it was: an elite shooting team that lost the defensive, rebounding and turnover battles almost every night.

report.headline: Second-best 3P% couldn't cover a defense, glass and turnovers that sank Milwaukee

recap.finish: 32-50, third in the Central; missed the postseason
recap.body:
This was a team with one real skill. Milwaukee made 38.7% of its threes, second in the league, took them at the fifth-highest rate, and posted the third-best eFG % at 56.5. A shooting profile like that usually anchors a top-ten offense. Instead the Bucks finished with an ORtg of 112.9, 24th, because almost everything else about their possessions was bottom-of-the-league: a 22.3 FT Rate (29th), a 21.1 ORB % (30th) and a 13.9 TOV % (28th). They made shots when they got them, but they didn't get enough of them.

The defense was the bigger problem. A DRtg of 119.3 ranked 27th and sat 3.6 points worse than the league average. Last season's DRtg was 113.4. Opponents shot 37.5% from three against them (28th), and the leaks came from the perimeter. Shooting guards scored 29.95 a game against Milwaukee (25th), and small forwards ranked near the bottom in rebounds, assists and threes allowed. Opposing centers were the exception: they scored 17.99 a game, the second-fewest allowed. The rim was mostly covered while the arc was not.

The arc of the season was a 4-1 October that never repeated. A 5-11 November dropped them to 9-12, and losing months in December and January left them at 18-28. February was the one real push: an 8-4 month brought them to 26-32 and within reach of respectability. Then March went 4-13, with scoring falling to 105.47 a game and 120.12 allowed, the worst month on both ends. The season never produced more than three straight wins, and it included a seven-game losing streak. April added a 2-5 finish, and the last 10 games went 3-7, with blowouts by Boston, Detroit and San Antonio.

The record was generous. A W vs Pt Diff of +6 ranked second in the league, and the -509 point differential implies 26 wins. The Bucks won close games at a rate that tends not to last, and the Net Rtg of -6.4 (25th) is a truer read than 32-50. They finished well behind Detroit and Cleveland in the division and only a game clear of Chicago.

The individual bright spot was Ryan Rollins. He played 2,376 minutes, ranked 16th of 89 on the point guard tab, and posted a team-best +8.5 On-Off. Kevin Porter Jr. ranked even higher, 10th, but appeared in only 38 games. Beyond them the grades were grim: backcourt D+, frontcourt D, wings D-. Gary Trent Jr. (-9.0 On-Off) and Ousmane Dieng (-9.5) took real minutes and lost them badly.

highlights.title: A genuinely elite shooting team
highlights.body: Milwaukee shot 38.7% from three, second in the league and 2.8 points above average, and ranked third in eFG %. That is not a one-year spike: last season's 3P% was the same 38.7, which makes it a stable trait of how this roster shoots. It is the one part of the profile worth building around.

highlights.title: Ryan Rollins carried the backcourt
highlights.body: Rollins led the team in minutes and points and ranked 16th of 89 on the point guard tab. The team was 8.5 points per 100 better with him on the floor, the best On-Off among the regulars. Kevin Porter Jr. graded even higher when available, but Rollins was the reliable one.

highlights.title: Opposing centers kept quiet
highlights.body: Centers scored 17.99 a game against Milwaukee, the second-fewest allowed, and grabbed the fourth-fewest rebounds. Myles Turner and Jericho Sims held the middle, and Sims added a 77.2 TS % on his limited touches. Whatever broke on defense, it wasn't the paint against bigs.

lowlights.title: Perimeter defense collapsed
lowlights.body: The DRtg of 119.3 ranked 27th, a steep drop from 113.4 a year earlier. Opponents shot 37.5% from three, 28th in the league. Shooting guards torched them for 29.95 a game, and wings got whatever they wanted. With a D- wing group and minus defenders in the guard rotation, this is a personnel problem, not a variance one.

lowlights.title: Losing the possession battle
lowlights.body: Milwaukee ranked 30th in ORB %, 29th in FT Rate and 28th in TOV %, so great shooting came on too few shots. These weaknesses compound: the offense rarely got second chances or free points and gave the ball away often. The FT Rate fell from 26.8 last season, which points to a roster that settled for jumpers.

lowlights.title: Even 32 wins was luck
lowlights.body: A W vs Pt Diff of +6, second in the league, means close games broke Milwaukee's way. The margin implies only 26 wins. The March collapse, 4-13 while allowing 120.12 a game, showed what the team looked like when the breaks stopped.

arc.note: After a 4-1 start, losing months in November through January buried them. An 8-4 February briefly pulled them to 26-32 before a 4-13 March and 2-5 April ended any doubt.

recap.nextYear: Carry the shooting and Rollins forward: the 3P% matched last season's, and Rollins graded as a top-20 point guard with the best On-Off on the team. Porter Jr. graded even better but played only 38 games, so his availability matters. Everything else needs work. The wing group graded D- and the listed wings barely played, which helps explain why opposing guards and wings ran free. The frontcourt graded D despite Portis and Turner holding up. The defense slid from a 113.4 DRtg to 119.3, and the team ranked near the bottom in rebounding, free throws and turnovers. Most important, the underlying team was closer to 26 wins than 32 given the +6 W vs Pt Diff. Expect regression from close-game luck unless the defense and possession numbers change.
